summary: The cluster is cheap: about 2 s on the JVM in total, of which PlutusConformanceJvmTest is 1.4 s, so there are no ci-time findings. The Plutus conformance corpus (1009 textual and .flat cases, exact budgets, all platforms) is the main guard of CEK semantics, and several hand-written suites repeat it: the success paths of CaseOnBuiltinsTest and the UPLC half of DropListTest duplicate corpus cases, and ConfiguredCryptoEvaluationTest compares evaluateScriptDebug with the very runWithBudgetTracking call it delegates to. Weak spots: the conformance failure arm accepts any host exception (F-32 pattern), the 'not thrown' test in ConfiguredEvaluationTest never reaches the catch-all, PlutusUseCasesBenchmarkTest and MachineParamsCostModelTest assert `!= null`, and the profiler/formatter tests check only titles and '> 0'. One main-bug candidate: MkCons promotes a non-constant head onto a (list value) to a VList, where Plutus fails (C24-1). Uncovered statements P4 need not chase: about 150 of Cek.scala's 277 are system-property-gated diagnostics (dumpCaseOnBuiltinDiag 981-1028, assertApplyDataToUc / assertCaseDataArity blocks 1300-1310, 1423-1436, 1517-1563, maxLamChainOnVar 1595-1626), 119 of ProfileFormatter's 310 are the unwired private inclusiveCosts (48-135), and BuiltinCostModel/CostModel/BuiltinValueOps belong to uplc.eval.budget and uplc.builtin.

findings.claim: The Scalus MkCons accepts a non-constant head when the list is a `(list value)` constant and returns a VList; Plutus 1.63 MkCons (PlutusCore/Default/Builtins.hs:1669-1683) takes both arguments as SomeConstant, so the reference machine fails with an unlifting error. A script that conses a native Constr onto a (list value) succeeds in Scalus (emulator, budget estimation) but fails on chain. The compiler emits (list value) element types for native-Constr representations (LoweredValueRepresentation.scala:534,924), so this is reachable from @UplcRepr(UplcConstr) code; whether a released contract hits it is unverified. Second defect in the same case: Builtin.scala:520 builds VList(elem :: Nil) and drops every element of a non-empty (list value) constant. The VList discharge path (Cek.scala:1744-1757) has no test at all.
findings.action: Test-only first: add a CEK test that evaluates [(force mkCons) (constr 0 []) (con (list value) [])] and asserts an evaluation failure (Plutus behavior), and one that conses a constr onto a non-empty (list value) and asserts the old elements are not lost. Owner decision: gate the VList extension off for ledger evaluation or remove it; if it stays, add a discharge test for an all-constant VList and for the IllegalStateException path.
findings.verification: Builtin.scala:505-525: the first MkCons case needs both args to be VCon. A non-VCon head (VConstr) goes to case 2 or 3. Case 3 (line 520-521) matches `VCon(Constant.List(DefaultUni.BuiltinValue, _))`, ignores the tail and returns `VList(elem :: Nil)`. So consing onto a non-empty (list value) loses every old element. DefaultUni.BuiltinValue is the CIP-153 `value` type (DefaultUni.scala:39, UplcParser.scala:158), so `(con (list value) [...])` with elements is a legal, parseable constant. Plutus Builtins.hs:1669-1683 (local clone ../iohk/plutus) types MkCons as `SomeConstant uni a -> SomeConstant uni [a]`. A constr head therefore fails unlifting on chain, but Scalus returns a success. Reachability: ProdUplcConstr/SumUplcConstr.defaultUni returns BuiltinValue (LoweredValueRepresentation.scala:534,924). SumBuiltinListEmitter.genNil (typegens/SumBuiltinListEmitter.scala:51-58) and ScalusRuntime.scala:868 emit `Constant.List(elementRepr.defaultUni(..), Nil)`. annotations.scala:85 documents `@UplcRepr(SumBuiltinList(UplcConstr))` as a user-facing option. No test under scalus-core/*/src/test mentions VList or `list value`, so the discharge path (Cek.scala:1744-1757) has no test. The proposed action adds tests only.

findings.claim: Same pattern as F-32: for an 'evaluation failure' case, assertOutcome accepts any Result.Failure, and evaluateDebug turns every Exception into one, so a host crash in Scalus (ClassCastException, MatchError, NPE outside a builtin) counts as conformance. Every machine error extends MachineError (Cek.scala:245-490). Also the Left("no file") budget arm silently skips the budget check, but all 1009 corpus cases have a .budget.expected file, so the arm is dead and would hide a lost budget file.
findings.action: In assertOutcome's failure arm, bind the exception and assert it is a MachineError (clue: class and message). Replace the Left("no file") arm with fail(s"no budget file"); expectationOf already treats a missing budget as an error.
findings.coverageRisk: none: stricter only; a case that now fails reveals a host crash

findings.claim: The test is named 'a cause the machine does not own is still reported as a failure, not thrown', but it never runs the catch-all in runWithBudgetTracking: the first half calls CekMachine.evaluateTerm and intercepts the thrown BuiltinError, the second half asserts success with the real logger. Mutation that survives: narrow PlutusVM.scala:189 to `case e: MachineError`. Only the JVM and JS ConfiguredCryptoEvaluationTest exercise this path (via a faulty platform), Native not at all.
findings.action: Add to the test: evaluate(integer, budgetSpender = a BudgetSpender whose spendBudget throws a sentinel IllegalStateException) and assert the result is a Result.Failure whose exception is the sentinel (eq). This is shared, so it covers JVM, JS and Native. Delete line 162-163 (asserts nothing about the claim).

findings.claim: Each test evaluates the same program twice, via evaluateScriptDebug ('legacy') and via runWithBudgetTracking(CountingBudgetSpender, tracing = true, validateResult = false), then asserts equal message, cause and budget. evaluateScriptDebug is runWithBudgetTracking(term, tracing = true, validateResult = true) with a CountingBudgetSpender (PlutusVM.scala:83-84, 142-155); validateResult only matters for a successful result, and every program here fails. The second evaluation is the same code path, so the equality assertions cannot fail. The 'legacy' naming is left over from a removed separate path. ConfiguredEvaluationTest:38 does the same for logs.
findings.action: In both ConfiguredCryptoEvaluationTest files keep one evaluation per test (vm.evaluateScriptDebug) with its message, cause and logs assertions; delete the runWithBudgetTracking blocks and the budget-equality asserts; rename 'legacy' to 'failure' in names and test titles. Delete ConfiguredEvaluationTest.scala:38.
findings.coverageRisk: none: the remaining evaluation runs the same runWithBudgetTracking code; message, cause identity and logs stay pinned
findings.verification:
The claim holds. evaluateScriptDebug is `runWithBudgetTracking(program.term, tracing = true, validateResult = true)` (PlutusVM.scala:83-84), and that overload goes through a fresh CountingBudgetSpender (PlutusVM.scala:142-155) to the same private[eval] method. validateResult is read only on success (PlutusVM.scala:177). Every crypto program fails, so the two runs follow the same code path and the budget/message equality asserts cannot fail. ConfiguredEvaluationTest.scala:38 is a success case with validateResult=true on both sides, so it is the same path too. The gap: in the JVM file, the cause assertion `failure.exception.asInstanceOf[BuiltinError].cause.getMessage == diagnostic` (jvm ConfiguredCryptoEvaluationTest.scala:39) exists only on the runWithBudgetTracking result. Deleting that block as written loses the cause check. In the JS file, cause and logs are already asserted on `legacy` (js lines 57, 61), and the sentinel-identity tests assert on both results.
Corrected action: before deleting the JVM runWithBudgetTracking block at lines 27-40, move the cause check onto `legacy`: `assert(legacy.exception.asInstanceOf[BuiltinError].cause.getMessage == diagnostic)`. The rest of the action stands: delete the duplicate evaluations, delete the budget-equality asserts and ConfiguredEvaluationTest:38, and rename 'legacy'.

findings.claim: Integer 0/1/2, negative, out of bounds, the 1001-branch Fibonacci table, and Constr tag 0/1/out-of-range are instances of one law: Case(scrutinee i, n branches) selects branch i iff 0 <= i < n, else fails with CaseIndexOutOfBounds (Integer) or MissingCaseBranch (Constr).
findings.action: Replace with two forAll properties: n <- choose(0, 1100), i <- frequency(inside [0, n), -1, n, n+k, large BigInt); branches are distinct integer constants; assert the selected constant or the exact exception class. Same for Constr(Word64(i), Nil) with i in the unsigned range, keeping the explicit >= 2^63 test at 204-229 as is.
findings.coverageRisk: none: covers every example value and the boundaries; keep the 2^63 and 2^32+1 Constr examples
findings.verification:
The law holds in main code. For Integer, Cek.scala:1314-1330 selects branch i iff `i >= 0 && i < cases.size`, else throws CaseIndexOutOfBounds. This includes n = 0 and BigInts far outside Int range. For Constr, Cek.scala:1284-1312 does an unsigned compare against maxIndexableTag, then `index < cases.size`, else throws MissingCaseBranch. The Fibonacci table (251-269, 1001 branches, n up to 1000) fits the proposed n <- 0..1100.
The gap: the cited range 169-197 also contains 'V4: Case on Constr with args applies them to lambda branch' (180-189). That test asserts that constructor fields are applied to a lambda branch: `Constr(1,[42])` with `\x -> x` gives 42. The proposed property generates only `Constr(Word64(i), Nil)` with constant branches, so it cannot produce that shape.
Corrected action: replace 27-77, 169-178, 191-197 and 251-269 with the two properties. Keep 180-189, and keep 204-229 as the finding says.

findings.claim: The nine Scala-builtin examples are instances of one oracle law: dropList(n, xs) == xs.drop(clamp(n)) with clamp(n) = 0 for n <= 0 and min(n, Int.MaxValue) otherwise. There are two implementations of dropList (the Scala-side Builtins.dropList and the CEK BuiltinRuntime) and no test checks that they agree.
findings.action: Replace 22-76 with one property: forAll (n: BigInt from a gen with 0, negatives, small positives, > Int.MaxValue, > Long.MaxValue; xs: List[BigInt] up to 20) assert Builtins.dropList(n, BuiltinList.from(xs)).toList == xs.drop(clamp(n)) and that the CEK result of [(force dropList) n xs] equals the same list.
findings.coverageRisk: none: the oracle covers every example; element-type variants (String, ByteString) do not change the code path
findings.verification:
Both implementations equal xs.drop(clamp(n)), with clamp = 0 for n <= 0 and min(n, Int.MaxValue) otherwise:
- Builtins.dropList (Builtins.scala:530-535): `if n.signum <= 0 then l else drop(if n.isValidInt then n.toInt else Int.MaxValue)`.
- CEK DropList (Builtin.scala:1239-1257): `dropCount = 0 if signum <= 0, n.toInt if valid Int, else Int.MaxValue`, then `ls.drop(dropCount)`.
The oracle holds for every list of up to 20 elements and every BigInt. The nine examples are covered: 0, -10, 3 of 5, all, 100 > len, empty list, Long.MaxValue. The String and ByteString examples use the same generic drop in both implementations, so element type does not change the path. No existing test compares the two implementations. Caveat for the implementer: huge n costs a lot of budget (IntegerCostedLiterally). Evaluate the CEK side with an unrestricted spender, such as Term.evaluateDebug with CountingBudgetSpender. Corpus dropList-09 shows that 10^19 evaluates fine that way.

findings.claim: About a dozen `.asInstanceOf[Result.Failure].exception.isInstanceOf[X]` casts (ConfiguredEvaluationTest, both ConfiguredCryptoEvaluationTest files) and six copies of a three-arm match `case Result.Failure(ex: X, ...) => ...; case Result.Failure(ex, ...) => fail(...); case _ => fail(...)` (CekSourcePosTest, SourceTraceTest). findings.claim: The property uses ScalaCheck's default Arbitrary[BigInt] (values up to about 256 bits, products of Longs), so it almost never hits the 64-bit word boundaries 2^(64k) - 1, 2^(64k), 2^(64k) + 1 where both formulas branch on bitLength / 64, and never values above 256 bits. Only k = 1 is checked by the example test (13-20).
findings.action: Use a local Gen mixing the default with ±(BigInt(2).pow(64 * k) + d) for k in 1..8 and d in {-1, 0, 1}, and random widths up to 1024 bits; the 2^64 example test then becomes redundant and can go.

findings.claim: Three tests compile and lower the same SIR (14-20, 39-45, 64-70); the first two are identical except evaluateScriptDebug vs evaluateScriptProfile. findings.action: Lower the SIR once into a val; loop the first two tests over the two evaluation methods; assert that the trace contains a position in SourceTraceTest.scala at the division line; use intercept[StackTraceMachineError] in the third test.

findings.claim: Result.alphaEq (used to compare evaluation results across backends) and Result.success have no test: the failure arm compares exception class, message, budget, costs and logs, and the mixed Success/Failure arm returns false.
findings.action: Add a small ResultTest: alpha-equivalent terms with equal budgets are alphaEq; a different budget or log is not; two failures with the same class and message are; Success vs Failure is not; success on a Failure throws NoSuchElementException.
